title: Vaudeville: Step Right Up!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore vaudeville, the American variety-show format that grew from French roots and its 19th and early 20th century heyday. They cover the etymology (Olivier Basselin and the Vire valley songs, chansons de vaudeville), the family-friendly rules enforced by B.F. Keith and E.F. Albee, "blue envelope" and blue comedy origins, vaudeville show structure (the "if you don't like it, wait a few minutes" motto, the second-to-last act slot, the haircut act), performer pay and the circuit business model, the racist and ethnic dialect acts alongside their leveling effect, black vaudeville stars such as Bert Williams, Mommie Pearl-style character Moms Mabley, and the TOBA circuit, Yiddish and Native American vaudeville, famous alumni such as Jack Benny, Will Rogers, and George Burns, and vaudeville's decline as movies took over. The episode ends with a plug for the show's Kiva lending team and Red Cross blood donation teams.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to vaudeville
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about the first whiff of fall, introduce the vaudeville topic suggested by Dave, and note that vaudeville gave birth to many later entertainment forms and was family friendly and widely popular.

segments.title: Etymology of the word vaudeville
segments.summary: The word traces to the Vire valley in France, where 15th-century satirical folk songs called chansons de vaudeville originated, associated with the poet Olivier Basselin. The name later shifted to Vau de Vire and then vaudeville, and America adopted the fancy French-sounding term.

segments.title: Origins, middle-class audience, and Benjamin Franklin Keith's rules
segments.summary: Vaudeville was aimed at a growing middle class, distinguishing itself from earlier bawdy, drunken European and American shows. Benjamin Franklin Keith and E.F. Albee, who opened the Bijou Theater in Boston, built circuits. Tony Pastor is credited with popularizing the term. Shows were family friendly, alcohol-free, and Keith enforced strict language rules, including sending a 'blue envelope' to offenders.

segments.title: Urbanization, working-class audiences, and the ethnic humor of vaudeville
segments.summary: After the Civil War America urbanized quickly, and cheap vaudeville offered immigrant workers an escape from long hours. Theater owners catered to neighborhoods. Ethnic dialect acts mocked many groups, but also served as a leveling and assimilating force, with performers often mocking their own ethnicity.

segments.title: Show structure, variety acts, and the handbook
segments.summary: Vaudeville bills were variety shows of 10 to 12 acts arranged deliberately, with the motto 'if you don't like it, wait a few minutes.' Acts included hobo acts, human calculators, electrical acts, statuary posing, and paper tearing. The opening act was the seating act, the second-to-last act was often the headliner, and the last act, the haircut act, was intentionally weak to clear the house.

segments.title: Black vaudeville, Bert Williams, and blackface
segments.summary: Discussion of racist ethnic stereotypes and blackface, with some black performers using blackface to satirize white performers. Bert Williams was the first black star of the Ziegfeld Follies, described by W.C. Fields as the funniest and saddest man, and reportedly worked himself to death at forty. Al Jolson was a major vaudeville star who used blackface and later starred in The Jazz Singer.

segments.title: Circuits, pay, and the TOBA and other vaudeville circuits
segments.summary: Circuits were the business model, with performers under exclusive contracts; top acts earned up to $3,000 a week. Performers worked two or more shows daily. The Theater Owners Booking Association (TOBA) ran the black vaudeville circuit, paid less than white circuits, and was jokingly called 'tough on black asses.' Butter Beans and Susie and Moms Mabley were stars; Yiddish and Native American vaudeville circuits also existed, including Fanny Brice's start.

segments.title: Famous alumni, movies, and vaudeville's decline
segments.summary: Stars who came out of vaudeville included Jack Benny, Fred Astaire, Will Rogers, Bob Hope, and George Burns. Movies were first shown as acts on vaudeville bills and eventually replaced vaudeville. Ed Sullivan reportedly said vaudeville had died a second death when his show was canceled in 1971. Vaudeville-style variety on early TV is noted, and the episode closes with plugs for the Kiva team and Red Cross blood donation teams.

segments.title: Sign-off and Kiva / Red Cross team plug
segments.summary: Hosts plug the Kiva micro-lending team and the Red Cross blood donation teams and sign off.
